title: Brahman, Atman and Moksha
welcome_lead: Approach the heart of Vedanta — the relationship between ultimate reality and the self.
meta_desc: IBDP Religious Studies Adventure: Brahman, atman, samsara, karma and moksha in Hindu thought.
final_note: You have walked the Vedantic path. The Hindu philosophical traditions are diverse and profound.

concepts.def: Ultimate reality, the unchanging, infinite ground of being in Hindu philosophy.
Eternal self or soul; in Advaita Vedanta, ultimately identical with Brahman.
Cycle of birth, death and rebirth in which atman is bound until liberation.
Law of moral cause and effect determining the conditions of rebirth.
Liberation from samsara — the highest aim of Hindu life.
Non-dualist school led by Adi Shankara (8th century) teaching identity of atman and Brahman.

walkthroughs.body_html: Brahman is described in the Upanishads as 'sat-chit-ananda' — being, consciousness and bliss. Beyond name and form (nirguna), Brahman is also accessible with qualities (saguna) through devotion to Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess. Different Vedanta schools — Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita — interpret the relationship differently.

Atman is the unchanging self bound to samsara through karma and ignorance (avidya). The aphorism 'Tat tvam asi' ('That thou art') from the Chandogya Upanishad expresses the Advaita identity of atman and Brahman, realised through knowledge (jnana).

Hindu traditions recognise multiple paths to moksha: karma yoga (selfless action), bhakti yoga (devotion), jnana yoga (knowledge) and raja yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita weaves these together; teachers like Ramanuja emphasised bhakti, while Shankara emphasised jnana.
